## 2. Condensed context — what already exists that this phase builds on

Real table/function names from Phases 1–3, so you extend what exists rather than inventing parallel structures:

- **Tenancy/roles**: `tenants` (has `tier smallint`, `gst_registered`, `default_consultation_fee`, `gstin`, `gst_state_code`), `profiles` (role enum: `pending, admin, doctor, nurse, billing, patient` — note there is still no `lab_tech` role; see §3.4). Helpers: `current_tenant_id()`, `current_user_role()`, `is_tenant_admin()`, `is_tenant_staff()`, `has_tenant_role(text[])`, `current_tenant_tier()`, `tenant_has_tier(int)`.
- **Clinical/OPD**: `patients`, `visits` (now carries `care_setting`, `admitted_at`, `discharged_at`, `bed_id`, `last_vitals_at`), `clinical_notes`, `prescriptions`/`prescription_items`, `drugs`/`drug_interactions`.
- **Billing**: `billing_line_items` (has `source_type`, `source_id`, `is_auto`, `tax_category`, `tax_rate`, `invoice_id`), `invoices` (has `subtotal`, `tax_total`, `grand_total`, `gstin_snapshot`, `status`, `issued_at`), `invoice_tax_lines`. `resolve_tax_treatment()` is the single source of truth for tax category/rate — reuse it, don't duplicate its logic.
- **Nursing/IPD**: `vitals`, `tasks`, `beds`, `medication_administrations`, `lab_orders`/`lab_results`, `lab_critical_ranges`. Views: `rounds_overview`, `critical_lab_alerts` (both `security_invoker`).
- **Established patterns you should keep using**: `{ok, code, message}` jsonb envelope for any RPC with branching/side effects, plain CRUD + RLS for simple reads, composite `(id, tenant_id)` FKs on every child table, column-level `GRANT`s withholding system-derived columns from clients, `SECURITY DEFINER` only where the acting user is deliberately not the right authority (documented each time), a negative-control step in every isolation test.

## 3. The main event: Phase 4 — Admin, Multi-Branch & Tier 3 Groundwork

**Goal, verbatim from `phases.md`:** Admin gets real visibility and control; groundwork laid for larger hospital tenants (OT, blood bank, insurance/TPA fields) without fully building them yet unless prioritized.

### 3.1 Admin dashboard aggregation

PRD §6.5: "Dashboard: patient volume, revenue, occupancy, staff utilization (scoped to their `tenant_id`)."

Design views or RPCs (your call, document which and why per metric — a simple scoped aggregate is a view; anything needing a date-range parameter or business-rule branching is an RPC) covering:
- **Patient volume**: new registrations and visit counts, by day/week/month. Source: `patients.created_at`, `visits.checked_in_at`.
- **Revenue**: from `invoices` (issued, not draft) — gross, by tax category if you want it to double as GST reporting groundwork, but that's a nice-to-have not a requirement this phase.
- **Occupancy**: Tier 2+ only, meaningfully — `beds` where `status='occupied'` vs total, and/or bed-days from `visits.admitted_at`/`discharged_at`. Decide whether this should be tier-gated (Tier 1 tenants have no beds, so the query would just return zero/empty — probably fine to leave ungated and let it naturally show nothing, matching the `beds` SELECT policy's own precedent of not gating reads. Your call, document it.).
- **Staff utilization**: this is the vaguest requirement in the PRD and you'll need to make a judgment call on what's actually measurable from existing data — e.g., consultations per doctor per day (from `visits.doctor_id` + `status='done'`), tasks completed per nurse (from `tasks.completed_by`). Don't invent a time-tracking system that doesn't exist. State plainly in your report and the contract file what you chose to measure and why, and what a real "utilization" metric would need that isn't in scope.

All of it: `security_invoker` views (same reason as `rounds_overview` — a definer view here would be a cross-tenant leak), scoped through `current_tenant_id()`, admin-only where the data itself isn't already role-appropriate for others to see incidentally.

### 3.2 User/role management RPCs (if anything is actually missing)

Check what already exists before building anything: `admin_set_user_role()` and `create_invite()`/`accept_invite()` already cover invite + role-change. `phases.md` asks for "invite, deactivate, change role" on the frontend side. **Deactivate does not exist yet on the backend.** Design it:
- A user cannot be deleted (medical records reference `profiles` via `ON DELETE RESTRICT` everywhere — this is deliberate, from Phase 2/3). "Deactivate" therefore needs to be a state, not a deletion — likely a `profiles.is_active boolean default true` (or similar) that RLS policies check alongside role, so a deactivated user's session (if not also revoked at the auth layer) can't act.
- Think through: does a deactivated admin's session get killed immediately, or just blocked on next RLS check? Supabase doesn't give you a clean server-side "kill this session now" primitive without hitting the Auth Admin API — decide whether this RPC should also call `auth.admin.signOut()`-equivalent logic (it can't from plain SQL; this may need to stay a plain column flag checked by RLS/RPCs, with actual session invalidation being a frontend/Auth-API concern you flag for Prince rather than solve here). Document your reasoning rather than silently picking one.
- The `CANNOT_DEMOTE_LAST_ADMIN` guard pattern from `admin_set_user_role()` almost certainly needs a sibling check here — you cannot deactivate the last active admin either.

### 3.3 Reconciliation logic

PRD §6.3 / `phases.md`: "compare `billing_line_items` vs. `invoices` for discrepancies."

Concretely, what needs to be detectable and surfaced (design the actual query/RPC, this list is the requirement, not the implementation):
- Pending charges not yet on any invoice (`billing_line_items.invoice_id IS NULL`) older than some staff-meaningful threshold — a charge sitting uninvoiced for days is the exact revenue leakage PRD §3 is about.
- An invoice whose line items don't sum to its stored `subtotal`/`tax_total`/`grand_total` — this should be structurally impossible if `create_invoice_for_visit()` is the only writer, but the whole point of a reconciliation view is to catch it if that invariant is ever violated (a service-role backfill, a manual dashboard edit, a future bug). Don't assume your own Phase 2 code is infallible; check it.
- Invoices with `amount_paid` inconsistent with `status` (e.g., marked paid but `amount_paid < grand_total`, or vice versa) — check the actual `invoices` schema/status enum from Phase 2 before assuming this column exists in the form you expect.

This is read-only reporting — an admin *sees* discrepancies, this phase does not need to auto-correct them. Design it as a view or RPC an admin can query for "is anything off, and what."

### 3.4 Audit log

PRD/`phases.md`: "who changed what, for compliance." This is the biggest genuinely new piece of infrastructure this phase adds, and several things already flagged it as needed:
- Phase 1's Memory.md noted "no audit log yet... there is no record of who changed whose role."
- Phase 3's migrations flagged medication administration corrections and DPDP-relevant access as belonging here.

Design:
- An `audit_log` table: `id`, `tenant_id`, `actor_id` (nullable — a trigger-driven system change may have no human actor), `action text`, `table_name text`, `row_id uuid`, `changes jsonb` (before/after or just after — decide and document; full before/after is more useful but doubles storage and risks capturing PII in the `jsonb` blob, which conflicts with rules.md §1.3 if a clinical note's content ends up in an audit row. **Think carefully about what you log for clinical tables specifically** — logging *that* a clinical note was edited, by whom, when, is compliance value; logging the note's *content* into an audit table is a second, less-guarded copy of PHI. Prefer logging metadata/diffs of non-clinical fields, or a redacted/field-name-only diff for clinical ones. State your choice explicitly.), `created_at`.
- RLS: admin-readable within their own tenant, no client write access at all — every row comes from a trigger or a `SECURITY DEFINER` function, same discipline as `tasks.is_auto`.
- Trigger scope for this phase — don't try to audit everything at once. Prioritize what's actually compliance-relevant and already flagged: `admin_set_user_role()` calls (who changed whose role), invite creation/acceptance, the new deactivate action from §3.2, and tenant settings changes (GST registration toggling, `tenants.name` changes). Extending to every clinical write is a larger effort than this phase needs — say so in your report if you scope it down, and what's left for later.
- Also: this is a natural moment to add the missing `lab_tech` role to `profiles`'s role enum if you judge it's cheap and low-risk to do now (Phase 3 flagged this gap). Not required — your call, but if Phase 3's closeout report (read it first) flagged this as more urgent than expected, address it here rather than deferring again indefinitely.

### 3.5 Tier 3 placeholder schema

`phases.md`: "Schema/RLS for `insurance_claims`, placeholder schema for `ot_schedule`, `blood_bank` (Tier 3, structure only)."

PRD §9 is explicit: **insurance underwriting/claims adjudication is out of scope — submission-format support only.** This means `insurance_claims` needs to hold enough structured data to *produce* a CGHS/ESIC/TPA-format submission (per PRD §6.3), not to process a claim's lifecycle, adjudicate it, or track approval/denial workflows. Keep this genuinely minimal — you are building a placeholder, not the claims module.

Suggested shapes, adjust and document changes as always:
- `insurance_claims`: `id`, `tenant_id`, `patient_id`, `visit_id`, `invoice_id` (nullable — a claim might be filed before final invoicing), `payer_type` (`cghs`/`esic`/`private_tpa`/etc.), `payer_name text`, `policy_or_beneficiary_number text`, `claim_amount numeric`, `status text` (keep this to submission states only — `draft`/`submitted`/`closed`, not an adjudication workflow with approve/reject/appeal states, since that's explicitly not being built), `submitted_at`, `notes`, timestamps. Composite FKs to `patients`/`visits`/`invoices` per the established pattern.
- `ot_schedule`: structure only, per phases.md. Minimal shape: `id`, `tenant_id`, `patient_id`, `visit_id`, `surgeon_id` (references `profiles`), `procedure_name text`, `scheduled_start`/`scheduled_end timestamptz`, `status text`, `ot_room text`. Tier 3 gated the same way `beds` is Tier 2 gated (`tenant_has_tier(3)` — you'll need this new helper, following `tenant_has_tier(2)`'s exact pattern from Phase 3).
- `blood_bank`: structure only. Minimal shape: something like a `blood_units` table (`id`, `tenant_id`, `blood_group text`, `component_type text` e.g. whole blood/plasma/platelets, `status text` e.g. available/reserved/issued/discarded, `collected_at`, `expires_at`) plus enough to link an issue to a patient/visit if you want the placeholder to be genuinely structurally useful rather than decorative. Keep it simple — this is groundwork, not a blood bank management system.

All three: RLS enabled from the migration that creates them (no exceptions, same as every phase before this), Tier 3 gated on write (reads can follow the `beds` precedent — ungated reads, gated writes — or you may decide reads should also be gated here since these are genuinely inactive/unused modules for Tier 1/2 tenants unlike `beds`; think about whether the "don't hide a bed a patient is in" argument that justified ungated `beds` reads even applies here, since nothing will ever be *in* an OT schedule or blood bank for a tenant that's never had the tier to use it — document whichever you choose).

### 3.6 Full error-handling audit against `rules.md` §3

This is a **review task across the whole backend**, not new code by default — though it may produce small fixes.

Go through every RPC written across Phases 1–4 (there are around 30 by now) and confirm against `rules.md` §3, point by point:
1. Every Supabase-reachable write path has RLS or a grant restricting it (spot-check a sample; you don't need to re-derive every policy from scratch, Phases 1–3 already did this rigorously).
2. No error path swallows silently. In particular check `EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` blocks (Phase 3's `flag_lab_result_critical()` has one, deliberately) — confirm each one logs something in the SQLSTATE/notes it stores rather than genuinely disappearing information.
3. Every business-rule failure returns a **stable, documented code** — cross-check that every code mentioned in every `docs/contracts/*.md` file actually exists in the code, and every code in the code is documented somewhere. This is the kind of drift-detection that's cheap to do now and expensive to discover later.
4. Clinical-safety-relevant failures fail loud — re-confirm `check_prescription_safety()`'s `partial`/`complete` split and `evaluate_lab_critical()`'s four-state vocabulary haven't regressed, and that nothing added this phase (the reconciliation view, the audit log) introduces a new place where "we couldn't check" could be confused with "checked, fine."
5. §3.7 (Edge Functions: structured `{error:{code,message}}`, never raw stack traces) — check `generate-prescription-pdf`, `generate-invoice-pdf`, `notify-critical-lab-value` all still comply.

Produce an actual findings list in your report — even if the finding is "audited N functions, found zero violations," say that explicitly rather than a vague "looks fine."

## 4. Boundaries (unchanged, repeated because they still apply)

1. Never bypass RLS; no service-role key outside a local dev script or a stated, narrow exception with a documented reason.
2. Never trust a client-passed `tenant_id`.
3. Never log patient PII/PHI — this phase's audit log is the highest-risk surface for this rule in the whole project so far. Re-read rules.md §1.3 before designing what goes into `audit_log.changes`.
4. No new backend server, ORM, or hosting provider.
5. Every table ships with RLS from the migration that creates it — including all three Tier 3 placeholder tables.
6. Migrations are additive history.
7. Do not touch `apps/web`.
8. Do not build OT scheduling, blood bank management, or insurance claim adjudication as working features — structure only, per §3.5. Do not build claims adjudication/approval workflows at all — PRD §9 rules this out entirely, not just for this phase.

- [ ] Admin can see real metrics (patient volume, revenue, occupancy, a documented staff-utilization proxy) scoped to their own tenant
- [ ] Reconciliation view/RPC correctly flags billing mismatches (pending charges, sum mismatches, payment-status inconsistencies)
- [ ] Tier 3 schema (`insurance_claims`, `ot_schedule`, `blood_bank`) exists, RLS-enabled, tier-gated, flagged clearly as structure-only
- [ ] Audit log table + triggers cover role changes, invite lifecycle, deactivation, and tenant-settings changes at minimum
- [ ] Full error-handling audit against `rules.md` §3 completed with an actual findings list
- [ ] User deactivation designed and implemented, with the session-invalidation question explicitly answered (even if the answer is "out of scope for the backend, flagged to Prince")
- [ ] Contract file(s) written for anything new that Prince needs to build against (admin dashboard queries, reconciliation, user management) — follow the established format
- [ ] `Memory.md` updated: decisions (§3), current state (§4), contracts (§5), risks (§6), scope notes for anything deliberately left as structure-only (§7)
- [ ] `supabase/types/database.types.ts` regenerated after these migrations are pushed
- [ ] Local test suite extended and passing (isolation tests for the three new Tier 3 tables at minimum, following the exact negative-control pattern every prior phase used)
